doc.title: Charles Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Spirituality in composing and playing
summary: Prompted by Cecil McBee's quote, Tolliver describes a spiritual connection to his musicians and rhythmic, drum-based inspiration for writing.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yes. I had a question that had to do with spirituality. And I think I’m guilty of for too long when people bring up spirituality I think of religion or faith. And I wanted to read something that Cecil McBee said in a conversation I had with him last November. And it was about spirituality and different periods in jazz. And he said, “well if it ain’t spiritual don’t play it. You know your spirit is what makes you play the instrument. If you’re not spiritual you ain’t feeling nothing. Elvin Jones used to say, ‘if you ain’t playing nothing get him off the stage and let someone else get up there and play it.’” So I don’t really have a question, Charles, but does spirituality play a role in your composing and in your playing? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

Oh yeah. I basically want to have a spiritual connection to the musicians that I’m performing with at the time and so I have their capabilities in mind. Sometimes when I’m writing something I says well so-and-so-and-so would probably like to solo off this or play this you know. So there is that spiritual connection to your fellow musicians you know, a lot when you’re writing songs you know if you are looking for some sort of inspiration. And my inspiration generally is rhythmical, dealing with the drums you know. Because I write a lot off of inspirational drum things.
Is there something that could happen in your day to day life that might inspire you to run to your staff paper or your computer or your keyboard or whatever, and start working on it?

Yeah. I mean that happens every day. A drum lick. I mean seriously you know it’s not necessarily going to the piano and you know saying oh what’s this little song that’s going on in my head. It generally is coming off some sort of rhythmical thing that I hear between the drums and the bass. And then I’ll put a melody to it and then chord changes if it needs some chord changes.
